prompt: Leucippus and Democritus called the small particles they believed made up all matter "atomos". What does the Greek word mean?

choices.text: Indivisible
Invisible
choices.why: "Atomos" comes from the Greek word for "indivisible": they thought atoms were the smallest pieces that matter could be split into.

choices.text: Element
choices.why: The "elements" were Aristotle's idea: fire, earth, air, and water. "Atomos" means indivisible.

choices.text: Charged
choices.why: Charge came into atomic theory more than two thousand years later. "Atomos" means indivisible.

explanation: In the fifth century BC, Leucippus and Democritus argued that all matter was made of small, finite particles they called atomos, from the Greek word for "indivisible".

prompt: What did the ancient Greek philosophers' ideas about atoms and "elements" have in common?

choices.text: They were philosophical concepts that were never tested by experiment
They were confirmed by careful measurements of mass
choices.why: The philosophers apparently never considered performing experiments to test their ideas.

choices.text: Both agreed that matter can be divided forever
choices.why: Leucippus and Democritus held that matter is made of indivisible atoms. It was Aristotle and others who thought matter could be infinitely divided.

choices.text: Both were quickly replaced by Dalton's theory
choices.why: Aristotle's view held sway for over two thousand years before Dalton.

explanation: The Greek philosophers thought about atoms and "elements" as philosophical concepts, but apparently never considered performing experiments to test their ideas. Aristotle's view, of four elements and infinitely divisible matter, held sway for over two thousand years.

prompt: Which of Dalton's postulates explains why the total mass stays the same when copper and oxygen react to form copper(II) oxide?

choices.text: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical change, only rearranged
Atoms of one element differ in properties from atoms of all other elements
choices.why: That postulate explains why elements differ. Mass is conserved because the atoms present before the change are all still present after it.

choices.text: A compound has atoms of its elements in a small, whole-number ratio
choices.why: That explains the fixed composition of copper(II) oxide, a 1:1 ratio, but not why the total mass stays the same.

choices.text: An atom is the smallest unit of an element that can take part in a chemical change
choices.why: Mass is conserved because no atoms are created or destroyed: they are only rearranged into new substances.

explanation: If atoms are neither created nor destroyed during a chemical change, but only rearranged, then the total mass of matter stays constant. This is the law of conservation of matter (or mass).

prompt: Soddy showed that atoms of the same element can differ in mass. Which of Dalton's postulates did this contradict?

choices.text: All atoms of an element have the same mass, characteristic of that element
Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical change
choices.why: Isotopes don't affect this: atoms are still conserved in chemical changes. What isotopes contradict is that all atoms of an element have the same mass.

choices.text: A compound has its elements' atoms in a fixed, small, whole-number ratio
choices.why: Isotopes are chemically identical, so compounds still have fixed ratios. What isotopes contradict is the idea of one mass per element.

choices.text: Matter is made of very small particles called atoms
choices.why: Isotopes are still atoms. They contradict the idea that all atoms of an element share one mass.

explanation: Dalton postulated that an element consists of one type of atom, with a mass that is the same for all atoms of that element. Isotopes, atoms of the same element that differ in mass, showed this isn't so.

prompt: What does the law of definite proportions (the law of constant composition) state?

choices.text: All samples of a pure compound contain the same elements in the same proportions by mass
Samples with the same mass ratio of elements are always the same compound
choices.why: This is the converse, and it isn't true in general: many compounds besides isooctane have a carbon-to-hydrogen mass ratio of 5.33:1.

choices.text: Two elements that form several compounds combine in mass ratios of small whole numbers
choices.why: That is the law of multiple proportions, about different compounds of the same two elements.

choices.text: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical change
choices.why: That is the law of conservation of mass.

explanation: Joseph Proust demonstrated that all samples of a pure compound contain the same elements in the same proportion by mass. Isooctane, for example, always has a carbon-to-hydrogen mass ratio of 5.33:1.

prompt: Every sample of isooctane has 5.33 g of carbon for each 1.00 g of hydrogen. How many grams of hydrogen are in a sample of isooctane that contains 26.65 g of carbon?
explanation: By the law of definite proportions the ratio is the same in every sample: 26.65 g C × (1.00 g H / 5.33 g C) = 5.00 g H.

prompt: An unknown liquid has a carbon-to-hydrogen mass ratio of 5.33:1, the same as isooctane. What can you conclude?

choices.text: It may or may not be isooctane: many compounds share this mass ratio
It must be isooctane, by the law of definite proportions
choices.why: The law works in one direction only. Every isooctane sample has this ratio, but samples with this ratio aren't necessarily isooctane.

choices.text: It can't be isooctane, because a different sample would have a different ratio
choices.why: Every sample of isooctane has the same ratio, so a matching ratio doesn't rule it out either.

explanation: All samples of a particular compound have the same mass ratio, but the converse is not true in general: samples with the same mass ratio aren't necessarily the same substance. Many compounds besides isooctane have a carbon-to-hydrogen mass ratio of 5.33:1.00.

prompt: Copper and chlorine form a green solid with 0.558 g chlorine per gram of copper, and a brown solid with 1.116 g chlorine per gram of copper. Which law do these data illustrate?

choices.text: The law of multiple proportions
The law of definite proportions
choices.why: That law is about samples of one compound. Here there are two different compounds of the same two elements, whose ratios compare as 2 to 1.

choices.text: The law of conservation of mass
choices.why: Conservation of mass is about total mass in a chemical change. These data compare two compounds of copper and chlorine.

explanation: When two elements form more than one compound, a fixed mass of one combines with masses of the other in a ratio of small whole numbers. Here (1.116 g Cl/g Cu) ÷ (0.558 g Cl/g Cu) = 2/1: the brown compound has twice as much chlorine per copper.

prompt: Two compounds of nitrogen and oxygen are analyzed. Compound 1 contains 0.571 g of oxygen per 1.00 g of nitrogen; compound 2 contains 2.86 g of oxygen per 1.00 g of nitrogen. What is the ratio of these ratios (compound 2 to compound 1), as a small whole number?
explanation: (2.86 g O/g N) ÷ (0.571 g O/g N) = 5.01, or 5. Compound 2 has five times as much oxygen per gram of nitrogen as compound 1: a small whole-number ratio, as the law of multiple proportions says.

prompt: Thomson's cathode ray was deflected toward a positive charge and away from a negative charge. What did he conclude?

choices.text: The particles in the ray are negatively charged
The particles in the ray are positively charged
choices.why: Unlike charges attract. Particles drawn toward a positive charge must be negative.

choices.text: The particles have no charge
choices.why: Uncharged particles wouldn't be deflected by electric charges at all.

choices.text: The particles are heavier than atoms
choices.why: Deflection by charges shows the sign of the charge. Thomson's charge-to-mass measurements showed the particles were much lighter than atoms, not heavier.

explanation: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract, so particles attracted by positive charges and repelled by negative charges must be negatively charged. Thomson's cathode ray particle is what we now call the electron.

prompt: Thomson found that the cathode ray had identical properties no matter which metal the electrodes were made of. Why did this matter?

choices.text: It suggested the particles were fundamental, subatomic constituents of all atoms
It showed that all metals are the same element
choices.why: Different metals are different elements. The point is that the particles were the same regardless of the source, so they must be part of every atom.

choices.text: It showed that the particles came from the air left in the tube
choices.why: Almost all the air was removed from the tube. Identical particles from every metal pointed to a constituent of all atoms.

choices.text: It proved that atoms are indivisible
choices.why: The opposite: particles lighter than atoms, found in every atom, showed that atoms are not indivisible.

explanation: Because the particles were less massive than atoms and indistinguishable regardless of the source material, Thomson proposed that they must be fundamental, subatomic constituents of all atoms: electrons.

prompt: What did Millikan conclude from finding that every oil drop's charge was a multiple of 1.6 × 10^−19 C?

choices.text: 1.6 × 10^−19 C is a fundamental charge: the charge of a single electron
Each oil drop held exactly one electron
choices.why: Drops had charges of 1, 2, 3, or more times 1.6 × 10^−19 C, from an excess of that many electrons.

choices.text: 1.6 × 10^−19 C is the mass of an electron
choices.why: Coulombs measure charge, not mass. The electron's mass came from combining Millikan's charge with Thomson's charge-to-mass ratio.

choices.text: Electrons have different charges in different oils
choices.why: The charges were always whole-number multiples of one value, which points to one fundamental charge.

explanation: Since the charge of a droplet was always a multiple of 1.6 × 10^−19 C, Millikan concluded that this is a fundamental charge, the charge of a single electron, with each drop carrying an excess of one, two, three, or more electrons.

prompt: In an experiment like Millikan's, an oil drop carries a charge of 8.0 × 10^−19 C. How many excess electrons does it carry?
explanation: Each electron carries 1.6 × 10^−19 C, so 8.0 × 10^−19 C ÷ 1.6 × 10^−19 C = 5 electrons.

prompt: Millikan measured the charge of an electron as 1.602 × 10^−19 C, and Thomson had measured its charge-to-mass ratio as 1.759 × 10^11 C/kg. What is the mass of an electron, in kilograms?
explanation: Mass = charge ÷ (charge-to-mass ratio) = 1.602 × 10^−19 C × (1 kg / 1.759 × 10^11 C) = 9.107 × 10^−31 kg.

prompt: What did Thomson's 1904 "plum pudding" model describe?

choices.text: A positively charged mass with electrons embedded in it, adding up to a neutral atom
A positive sphere surrounded by a ring of electrons, like Saturn
choices.why: That was Hantaro Nagaoka's competing model, from 1903.

choices.text: A tiny, dense, positive nucleus surrounded by mostly empty space
choices.why: That was Rutherford's nuclear model, which came later, from the gold foil experiments.

choices.text: Electrons in circular orbits with only certain allowed radii
choices.why: That was Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, from 1913.

explanation: Thomson's plum pudding model described a positively charged mass with an equal amount of negative charge, in the form of electrons, embedded in it, since all atoms are electrically neutral.

prompt: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, most α particles passed straight through the foil without being deflected. What did Rutherford deduce from this?

choices.text: An atom's volume is mostly empty space
Gold atoms have no positive charge
choices.why: A few α particles were deflected sharply, which showed a highly concentrated positive charge. The undeflected majority showed the atom is mostly empty space.

choices.text: The foil was too thin to contain any atoms
choices.why: The foil was very thin, but it was still made of gold atoms. The particles passed through essentially empty space inside those atoms.

choices.text: α particles have no charge
choices.why: α particles are positively charged: two protons and two neutrons. That is why the few that came close to a nucleus were repelled.

explanation: Because most of the fast-moving α particles passed through the gold atoms undeflected, they must have traveled through essentially empty space inside the atom. Rutherford concluded that an atom's volume is mostly empty space.

prompt: A very small number of α particles bounced almost straight back from the gold foil. What did this show?

choices.text: Each atom has a small, heavy, positively charged nucleus at its center
Positive charge is spread evenly through each atom, as in plum pudding
choices.why: Spread-out charge couldn't turn back a fast α particle. Only a highly concentrated positive charge could.

choices.text: The α particles hit electrons, which knocked them back
choices.why: Electrons are far too light to deflect the rapidly moving α particles. The deflections came from the much heavier nucleus.

choices.text: Gold atoms are packed with no space between them
choices.why: Most α particles passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space. The rare rebounds came from tiny, dense nuclei.

explanation: Like charges repel, so the few positive α particles that changed path abruptly must have hit or closely approached a body with a highly concentrated positive charge. Since this happened rarely, that charge occupies only a small amount of space: a small, relatively heavy, positively charged nucleus at the center of each atom.

prompt: Mesothorium, thought to be a new element, turned out to be chemically identical to radium but different in atomic mass. What did findings like this lead Soddy to realize?

choices.text: An element can have atoms of different masses that are chemically indistinguishable: isotopes
Mesothorium and radium are two different elements with the same properties
choices.why: Being chemically identical made them the same element. Soddy realized one element can have atoms of different masses.

choices.text: Atomic masses can't be measured accurately
choices.why: The masses were measured correctly and really differ. Soddy's insight was that one element can have atoms of different masses.

choices.text: Atoms change mass when they take part in a chemical change
choices.why: The different masses belong to different types of atom of the same element, not to atoms changing in reactions.

explanation: Results like mesothorium's led Frederick Soddy to realize that an element could have types of atoms with different masses that were chemically indistinguishable. These are isotopes, and Soddy won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1921 for the discovery.

prompt: How did Chadwick's 1932 discovery of the neutron explain isotopes?

choices.text: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
Isotopes have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
choices.why: This is reversed. The number of protons decides the element and its chemistry, so isotopes share it; they differ in neutrons.

choices.text: Isotopes have different numbers of electrons
choices.why: Electrons have negligible mass, and isotopes are chemically identical. They differ in mass because of their neutrons.

choices.text: Neutrons give isotopes different chemical properties
choices.why: Isotopes are chemically identical. Neutrons change only their mass.

explanation: Isotopes differ in mass because they have different numbers of neutrons, but they are chemically identical because they have the same number of protons.

prompt: What pattern did John Newlands find when he arranged the known elements in order of increasing atomic mass?

choices.text: Every seventh element had similar properties: his "law of octaves"
Elements fell into triads of three with similar properties
choices.why: Triads were Johannes Dobereiner's idea, for example chlorine, bromine, and iodine.

choices.text: Atomic volume rose and fell periodically
choices.why: That was Lothar Meyer's approach, plotting atomic volume against atomic mass.

choices.text: Order by atomic number, not atomic mass, fixed the misplaced elements
choices.why: That was Moseley's discovery, in 1913, from x-ray frequencies.

explanation: Newlands arranged the elements by increasing atomic mass and found that every seventh element had similar properties, so he proposed classifying them into octaves. The law didn't seem to work for elements heavier than calcium.

prompt: What was the key difference between Mendeleev's periodic table and those of Meyer and others?

choices.text: Mendeleev didn't assume all the elements were known, and left blanks for undiscovered ones
Mendeleev ordered the elements by atomic number
choices.why: Atomic number came later, from Moseley in 1913. Mendeleev worked with atomic masses.

choices.text: Mendeleev included the noble gases
choices.why: The noble gases were absent from Mendeleev's table; they were discovered more than 20 years later.

choices.text: Mendeleev arranged the elements in octaves
choices.why: Octaves were Newlands's idea. Mendeleev's key step was leaving blanks for elements not yet discovered.

explanation: Mendeleev did not assume that all the elements had been discovered; only about two-thirds of the naturally occurring elements were known. He deliberately left blanks at atomic masses 44, 68, 72, and 100, for elements now known as scandium, gallium, germanium, and technetium.

prompt: Mendeleev predicted an element he called eka-silicon, to fill a blank below silicon. Which element turned out to fill it?

choices.text: Germanium
Gallium
choices.why: Gallium matched eka-aluminum, the blank below aluminum.

choices.text: Scandium
choices.why: Scandium filled Mendeleev's blank at atomic mass 44. Eka-silicon, at 72, turned out to be germanium.

choices.text: Technetium
choices.why: Technetium filled the blank at atomic mass 100. Eka-silicon, at 72, turned out to be germanium.

explanation: The observed properties of gallium and germanium matched Mendeleev's predictions for eka-aluminum and eka-silicon so well that his periodic table rapidly gained acceptance once they were discovered.

prompt: Indium's atomic mass was first reported as 75.6, assuming its oxide was InO. Mendeleev argued the oxide was really In2O3. Keeping the same mass ratio of indium to oxygen, what atomic mass does In2O3 give for indium?
explanation: With InO, one indium atom pairs with one oxygen atom, giving 75.6. In In2O3, two indium atoms share the mass that goes with three oxygen atoms, so each indium atom has 75.6 × 3/2 = 113.4, or about 113, which places indium among the metals, between cadmium and tin.

prompt: Meyer's "atomic volume" is what we now call molar volume. An element has a molar mass of 24.31 g/mol and a density of 1.74 g/cm^3. What is its molar volume?
explanation: Molar volume = molar mass ÷ density = (24.31 g/mol) ÷ (1.74 g/cm^3) = 13.97 cm^3/mol.

prompt: Argon has a larger atomic mass than potassium (39.9 versus 39.1 amu), yet it comes before potassium in the periodic table. What did Moseley show that explains this?

choices.text: The elements are ordered by atomic number, and argon's (18) is lower than potassium's (19)
Argon's atomic mass had been measured incorrectly
choices.why: Argon's atomic mass really is greater than potassium's. Moseley showed that the order depends on atomic number instead.

choices.text: Noble gases are always placed before metals, whatever their mass
choices.why: There is no such rule. The order follows atomic number, and argon's is 18, potassium's 19.

choices.text: The elements are ordered by density
choices.why: Moseley showed that the underlying order is atomic number, the number of protons in the nucleus.

explanation: In 1913, analyzing the frequencies of x-rays emitted by the elements, Moseley found that the order of the elements is based on atomic number Z, the number of protons in the nucleus, not atomic mass. Argon's Z is 18 and potassium's is 19, so they were placed correctly.

prompt: Bohr's 1913 model explained hydrogen's emission spectrum with one assumption. What was it?

choices.text: The electron moves around the nucleus in circular orbits with only certain allowed radii
The electron is spread evenly through a positive sphere
choices.why: That resembles Thomson's plum pudding model. Bohr assumed circular orbits with only certain allowed radii.

choices.text: The electron can orbit at any distance from the nucleus
choices.why: Bohr's key step was the opposite: only certain radii, and so certain energies, are allowed.

choices.text: The electron sits motionless in the nucleus
choices.why: In Bohr's model the electron moves around the nucleus, in orbits with only certain allowed radii.

explanation: Bohr's model required only one assumption: the electron moves around the nucleus in circular orbits that can have only certain allowed radii. We now know circular orbits are incorrect, but the idea that the electron can occupy only certain regions of space held.

prompt: Use the Rydberg equation, 1/λ = RH (1/nl^2 − 1/nh^2), with RH = 1.097 × 10^7 m^−1, to find the wavelength in nanometers of the hydrogen emission line for the transition from n = 7 to n = 2.
In hydrogen's emission spectrum, the Lyman series ends at n = 1 and the Paschen series at n = 3. In which regions of the spectrum do their lines appear?

choices.text: Lyman in the ultraviolet; Paschen in the infrared
Lyman in the infrared; Paschen in the ultraviolet
choices.why: This is reversed. Transitions to n = 1 release a great deal of energy, giving ultraviolet light; transitions to n = 3 release much less, giving infrared.

choices.text: Both in the visible
choices.why: The visible lines are the Balmer series, which ends at n = 2.

choices.text: Lyman in the visible; Paschen in the ultraviolet
choices.why: The visible lines are the Balmer series (to n = 2). Lyman lines are ultraviolet and Paschen lines infrared.

explanation: Transitions down to n = 1 (Lyman) release a great deal of energy, corresponding to ultraviolet light. Transitions to n = 3, 4, and 5 (Paschen, Brackett, and Pfund) release much less, corresponding to infrared. The Balmer series, ending at n = 2, is visible.

prompt: Bohr's model worked only for species that contain a single electron. Which of these could it describe?

choices.text: He^+
He
choices.why: A neutral helium atom has two electrons, and Bohr's model couldn't explain the spectrum of any element other than hydrogen.

choices.text: Li
choices.why: A neutral lithium atom has three electrons. Bohr's model worked only for one-electron species such as H, He^+, and Li^2+.

choices.text: H2
choices.why: H2 is a molecule with two electrons. Bohr's model worked only for one-electron species.

explanation: Bohr's model could not quantitatively explain the emission spectra of any element other than hydrogen; it worked only for species with just one electron, such as H, He^+, and Li^2+.

prompt: White light passes through hydrogen gas and then through a prism. Where do the dark lines of hydrogen's absorption spectrum appear?

choices.text: At the same wavelengths as the bright lines of its emission spectrum
At wavelengths halfway between its emission lines
choices.why: Absorption and emission involve the same pairs of energy levels, so the dark lines sit exactly where the bright emission lines are.

choices.text: Nowhere: hydrogen absorbs all wavelengths equally
choices.why: Atoms absorb only the specific energies that match the differences between their energy levels.

choices.text: Only in the infrared
choices.why: Hydrogen's absorption lines include the visible 656, 486, 434, and 410 nm, the same as its Balmer emission lines.

explanation: Hydrogen atoms absorb light whose energy matches the gaps between energy levels, producing dark lines at 656, 486, 434, and 410 nm, the same positions as its emission lines. Emission and absorption spectra are essentially complementary images.
